facts: A **square** has $4$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of **order $4$**.
A **non-square rectangle** has $2$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of **order $2$**.
A **non-square rhombus** has $2$ lines of symmetry (its diagonals) and order $2$.
A general **parallelogram** has **no** lines of symmetry but rotational symmetry of order $2$.
steps: For a line of symmetry, imagine folding along the dashed line — do the halves match?
For rotational symmetry, count how many turns in one full circle give the same picture.
Match the shape to its known symmetry properties.

workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) The vertical midline is a line of symmetry: folding along it puts the left half exactly on the right half. Folding along $AC$ does not make the halves match.
(b) The horizontal midline is also a fold line. There are $2$ lines of symmetry.

workedExamples.question_text:
This is a non-square rhombus.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.75,every node/.style={font=\normalsize,text=black}]
\draw[black] (0,-1.6)--(2.9,0)--(0,1.6)--(-2.9,0)--cycle;
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
(a) Does it match its starting position after each turn about its centre: $90^{\circ}$, $180^{\circ}$, $270^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$?
(b) State its rotational order and identify its lines of symmetry.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) No, yes, no, yes. A half-turn puts each vertex on the opposite vertex. A quarter-turn does not match the longer and shorter diagonals.
(b) It matches twice during one full turn, so its rotational order is $2$. Its two diagonals are its $2$ lines of symmetry.

workedExamples.question_text:
This general parallelogram is neither a rectangle nor a rhombus.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.75,every node/.style={font=\normalsize,text=black}]
\draw[black] (0,0)--(4.5,0)--(5.8,2.2)--(1.3,2.2)--cycle;
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
(a) State the number of lines of symmetry.
(b) State the order of rotational symmetry.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) No fold makes the halves match, so there are $0$ lines of symmetry.
(b) A $180^{\circ}$ turn maps the parallelogram onto itself. It matches twice during one full turn, so its rotational order is $2$.

foundation.solution_text:
A square folds onto itself along its vertical and horizontal midlines and along both diagonals.
It has $4$ lines of symmetry.

The vertical and horizontal midlines are fold lines, but the diagonals are not.
It has $2$ lines of symmetry.

Each diagonal divides the rhombus into matching halves.
It has $2$ lines of symmetry.

Only the vertical diagonal folds the left half onto the right half.
It has $1$ line of symmetry.

No vertical, horizontal or diagonal fold makes the two halves match.
It has $0$ lines of symmetry.

The rectangle matches its starting position after a $180^{\circ}$ turn and after a full turn.
Its rotational symmetry is order $2$.

development.solution_text:
The square matches after turns of $90^{\circ}$, $180^{\circ}$, $270^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$.
Its rotational symmetry is order $4$.

A $180^{\circ}$ turn maps every vertex onto the opposite vertex.
Its rotational symmetry is order $2$.

No turn less than a full turn maps the unequal top and bottom vertices onto matching positions.
Its rotational symmetry is order $1$.

No fold line matches the two halves, so there are $0$ lines of symmetry.
A $180^{\circ}$ turn does match the shape, so the rotational symmetry is order $2$.

Folding along $EF$ swaps the left and right halves, and folding along $GH$ swaps the top and bottom halves.
The diagonals do not fold a non-square rectangle onto itself.
$EF$ and $GH$ are the lines of symmetry.

Both diagonals and both lines joining midpoints of opposite sides are fold lines, so there are $4$ lines of symmetry.
The square matches after turns of $90^{\circ}$, $180^{\circ}$, $270^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$, so its rotational order is $4$.

mastery.solution_text:
$AC$ and $BD$ are lines of symmetry: folding along either diagonal makes the halves match.
Folding along $EF$ or $GH$ does not make the halves match.

The diagonal joining the two unequal-angle vertices folds the two halves onto each other, so there is $1$ line of symmetry.
The kite matches only after a full turn, so its rotational order is $1$.

mastery.question_text: Draw a trapezium with exactly one pair of parallel sides and no axes of symmetry.
mastery.solution_text:
One possible trapezium is shown below.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\draw (0,0)--(5.2,0)--(3.8,2.1)--(0.6,2.1)--cycle;
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
The top and bottom sides are parallel. The unequal sloping sides prevent a fold line from making the halves match, so there are $0$ axes of symmetry.
